source_text: ἡγιάσθητε ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ ἐν τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν.» ἄθρει οὖν, ἄθρει, ὡς εἰ θεϊκὸν ὄνομα, ὥσπερ οὖν θεϊκόν, τὸ τοῦ υἱοῦ, ἐξάπαντος καὶ τὸ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος· ἓν γὰρ ἀμφοῖν αὐτῶν ἐδήλωσεν ὄνομα. καὶ ὅτι, ὡς συγκτίσαν ἀρρήτως τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα παρὰ τὴν ἀρχὴν καὶ νῦν ἀνακτίζει. τὸ γὰρ ἀπολούσασθαι, τὸ ἀνακτισθῆναι ἐσήμανεν. Τίτῳ δέ· «ἀναγεννήσας ἡμᾶς διὰ λουτροῦ παλιγγενεσίας καὶ ἀνακαινώσεως πνεύματος ἁγίου.» οὐδὲν δὲ ἧττον καὶ ὁ ἱεροψάλτης τοὺς ἤδη ἐν γενέσει ὑπάρχοντας νῦν κτιζομένους ἐν τῇ θείᾳ κολυμβήθρᾳ πνευματικῶς ἀξιοῖ εἰδέναι. φησὶν γάρ· «λαὸς ὁ κτιζόμενος αἰνέσει τὸν κύριον.» οὔκουν αἱ τὴν αὐτὴν τιμὴν καὶ ἐνέργειαν ἔχουσαι ὑποστάσεις τὴν αὐτὴν ἐκληρώσαντο φύσιν, καὶ οὐδὲν θεότητι καὶ δυνάμει διαφέρουσιν ἀλλήλων, μόναι δὲ συμφύεσθαι καὶ συντάττεσθαι καὶ πανταχοῦ συνεπινοεῖσθαι δύνανται τῷ ἑνί· ὃς ἄμφω αὐτός, οὐχ ὧν αἱ ὑποστάσεις ἀμφοῖν, ἔχει ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ ἀνάρχως καὶ ἐξ ἴσου καὶ ὁμοίου καὶ ἀλέκτως ἡνωμένας καὶ συνεχεῖς τὰς ὑποστάσεις. ἔτι πρὸς τοῖς λεχθεῖσιν· πᾶν δικαίωμα τῶν αἱρετικῶν τούτων ὁμοιότροπον, ὥσπερ καὶ ὁμοιόλεκτόν ἐστι τῆς νῦν κινουμένης ἑώλου αὐτῶν σοφιστείας, ὡς μαθησόμεθα μετ' οὐ πολὺ τῇ πείρᾳ ἐξ αὐτῶν τῶν κεφαλαίων. εἰ γὰρ τυχὸν λέξιν τινά, ὡς τὴν «αἰώνιος» ἢ τὴν «ἀγαθός», θείαν ἔνδειξιν κομίζουσαν περὶ τῆς ἐν μονάδι τριάδος, καὶ αὐτῇ καθ' ὅλου καὶ τελείως προσήκουσαν, ἔτυχέν που εἰρῆσθαι περὶ κτίσματος, μετὰ τῆς ὀφειλομένης κτίσματι μνήμης, οὐδὲν μὲν λέγουσιν τί γὰρ καὶ εἰπεῖν ἔχουσιν; περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ· κατάγουσι δὲ εὐθὺς ἀφρονέστατα τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα εἰς τὴν κτίσιν, οὐκ ἀνάγουσι πρεπωδέστατα εἰς τὸν θεὸν καὶ τὸν μονογενῆ τοὺς ἐν ὁμοίῳ καὶ ἴσῳ τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι ἁρμοδιώτατα ὑπὸ τῶν θεολόγων ἀνευφημηθέντας. καὶ μόνων τοίνυν τῶν πρὸς ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ κεφαλαίῳ ᾧ μέτειμεν, δικαιολογηθέντων ὑπερβαθῆναι μὴ δυναμένων, ἀρκούντων δὲ εἰς ὅλον τὸν περὶ αἱρετικῶν ἀγῶνα· ἢ δειξάτωσαν ὃ καὶ λέγειν βαρὺ λίαν, ὡς ἀρχὴ ἢ πέρας τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος κεχρησμῴδηταί που· ἢ ὅλως, ὅτι ὁδόν τινα ἔσχεν ἐπὶ φθορὰν ὡς ἡ ἀγγελικὴ καὶ ἀνθρωπικὴ προαίρεσις· ἢ ἔστω αὐτοῖς, τὸ δὴ λεγόμενον, «βοῦς ἐπὶ γλῶσσαν». τοσαῦτα μὲν περὶ ἐκείνων ἐγὼ δὲ ἐπὶ τὴν ἐξ ἀρχῆς ὑπόθεσιν μεταβήσομαι. 6.5ν ὅτι ὡς ἄτρεπτον ἀρετῆς τε κακίας τε ἀνεπίδεκτόν ἐστιν. ἡ κτίσις ἡ λογικὴ ἀρετῆς τε καὶ κακίας ἐστιν δεκτική, ὡς εὑρίσκομεν ἐν ἀσωμάτοις μέν, καθὰ προείπομεν, ἀρετῆς ἐντὸς τοὺς εὐδοκίμους ἀγγέλους, κακίας δὲ τοὺς ἐκριφέντας· ἐν δὲ σώμασιν, ὡς ἐσμὲν ἡμεῖς αὐτοί. τὸ δὲ θεϊκὸν πνεῦμα ὑπὲρ ἀρετὴν καὶ δόξαν τυγχάνον, μᾶλλον δ' αὐτὸ πηγάζον τὴν ἀκροτάτην ἀρετήν, οὐδενός ἐστι τούτων δεκτικόν, ὡς οὐδὲ ὁ πατὴρ οὐδ' ὁ υἱός. εἰ δὲ μὴ δεκτικόν, οὐδ' ἑτερόβουλον· εἰ δὲ τοῦτο ποιεῖ γὰρ πανθ' ὅσα θέλει ὁ πατήρ, οὐδ' ἑτεροούσιον. κἀντεῦθεν οὖν συνάγεται καὶ τό τε μὴ εἶναι αὐτὸ κτίσμα, ἀπαραλλάκτως δὲ ἔχειν πρὸς τὸν θεὸν πατέρα καὶ τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸ ἡμᾶς ἐξ αὐτοῦ τὸν θεόν, ἐξ οὗ φυσικῶς ἐξεπορεύθη, γινώσκειν, ὅτι καὶ ἐν ἡμῖν ἐστιν ὡς γέγραπται. 6.6ν ὅτι φύσει ἅγιον καὶ ἁγιάζον καὶ δικαιοῦν ἡ κτίσις ἁγιάζεται καὶ δικαιοῦται ὑπὸ τοῦ τὴν φύσιν ἁγίου θεοῦ· δεκτικὴ γὰρ τοῦ ἁγιασθῆναι καὶ δικαιωθῆναι τυγχάνει, οὐ παρεκτική. τὸ δ' ἅγιον πνεῦμα, ἐπείπερ διέστηκε· μὲν τῆς κτίσεως, συνῆπται δὲ τῇ φύσει ἐκείνῳ, ἐξ οὗ ἐκπεπόρευται περὶ οὗ καὶ ἐμυσταγωγήθημεν, ὡς· «πᾶσα δόσις ἀγαθὴ καὶ πᾶν δώρημα τέλειον ἄνωθέν ἐστι, κατα βαῖνον ἐκ τοῦ πατρὸς τῶν φώτων, παρ' ᾧ οὐκ ἔστι παραλλαγὴ ἢ τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα». καὶ ἐπείπερ πάντων κήδεται καὶ προμηθεῖται καὶ αὐτῶν τῶν ὑπαιτίων· ἁγιάζει μὲν καὶ δικαιοῖ καὶ σοφίζει καὶ πᾶν εἶδος ἐπουρανίου ἀρετῆς παρέχει· αὐτὸ δὲ οὐδαμῶς εὑρίσκεται ἔχον ἐπιτηδειότητα τοῦ ἁγιάζεσθαι ἢ 59 δικαιοῦσθαι ἢ σοφίζεσθαι ὑφ' ἑτέρου καθὰ οὐδ' ὁ αὐτοφυὴς πατὴρ οὐδ' ὁ ὁμοφυὴς αὐτοῦ υἱός· ὡς καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ὀρθῶς εὐφημεῖσθαι αὐτοάγιόν τε καὶ «πνεῦμα ἁγιοσύνης», ἀντὶ τοῦ, φύσει καὶ ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ ἅγιον· καὶ «πνεῦμα θεῖον», ἀντὶ τοῦ, φύσει θεός· καὶ «πνοὴ παντοκράτορος», ἀντὶ τοῦ, ὁμοούσιον τοῦ παντοκράτορος πνευσθὲν ἐκ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ· ὥστε καὶ μόνην μίαν τοιαύτην ὀνομασίαν δεικνύναι αὐτὸ ὁμοούσιόν τε τῷ θεῷ πατρὶ καὶ ἁγιαστικὸν καὶ μηδὲ λόγῳ χωρεῖσθαι. τοιγάρτοι ὁ δυνατὸς εἰπεῖν τε καὶ τύπους ἐκθέσθαι πίστεως Παῦλος
pass_a_gloss: [...] you were sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God.' Look then, look, that if the name of the Son is divine, as indeed it is divine, wholly so is that of the Holy Spirit too; for he made plain one name of both of them. And that, as having ineffably co-created at the beginning, the Holy Spirit now also re-creates. For 'to be washed' signified 'to be created again'. And to Titus: 'having begotten us again through a washing of rebirth and renewal of the Holy Spirit.' And no less the sacred psalmist too deems it right to know those already existing in birth as now being created spiritually in the divine pool (font). For he says: 'a people being created will praise the Lord.' So then the hypostases having the same honour and working have received by lot the same nature, and differ from each other in nothing in Godhead and power, and alone are able to grow together with and be ranked with and everywhere be thought together with the One; who has both, he himself not being (copy-text: of whom) the hypostases of both, out of himself without beginning and on equal and like terms and unspeakably united and continuous, the hypostases. Further, besides the things said: every plea of these heretics is of like fashion, as also of like wording, with their stale sophistry now set moving, as we shall learn not much later by trial out of the chapters themselves. For if perhaps some word, like 'eternal' or 'good', carrying a divine indication about the Trinity in a unity, and belonging to it wholly and perfectly, happened somewhere to be said about a creature, with the mention owed to a creature, they say nothing (for what indeed do they have to say?) about God the Father and his Son; but they straightway most senselessly lead down the Holy Spirit into the creation, they do not lead him up most fittingly to God and the Only-begotten, who were most aptly acclaimed by the theologians in like and equal terms with the Holy Spirit. And so, the things argued by us in the chapter which we are pursuing being alone unable to be stepped over, and sufficing for the whole contest about heretics: either let them show, which is very heavy even to say, that a beginning or end of the Holy Spirit has been uttered in oracle somewhere; or at all, that he had some road toward corruption as the angelic and human choice; or let there be for them, as is said, 'an ox upon the tongue'. So much about those; but I will cross over to the subject from the beginning. 6.5ν [Chapter title:] That as unchangeable he is not receptive of virtue and vice. The rational creation is receptive of both virtue and vice, as we find among the bodiless, as we said before, the approved angels within virtue, and the ones thrown out within vice; and among bodies, as we ourselves are. But the divine Spirit, being above virtue and glory, or rather himself welling up the highest virtue, is receptive of none of these, as neither the Father nor the Son. And if not receptive, not of another will either; and if this (for he does all things whatever the Father wills), not of another substance either. And from here then is gathered both his not being a creature, but holding without variation toward God the Father and his Son, and our knowing from him God, out of whom he proceeded by nature, that he is also in us, as it is written. 6.6ν [Chapter title:] That he is holy by nature and sanctifying and justifying. The creation is sanctified and justified by the God holy by nature; for it is receptive of being sanctified and justified, not bestowing. But the Holy Spirit, since he stands apart on the one hand from the creation, but has been joined by nature to that one out of whom he has proceeded (about whom we were also initiated, as: 'every good giving and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning'), and since he cares and provides for all, even the guilty themselves: on the one hand he sanctifies and justifies and makes wise and furnishes every form of heavenly virtue; but he himself is in no way found having fitness for being sanctified or (printed page 59 here) justified or made wise by another, just as neither the self-grown Father nor his Son of like nature; so that for this too he is rightly spoken of as self-holy and 'Spirit of holiness', in place of: holy by nature and from himself; and 'divine Spirit', in place of: God by nature; and 'breath of the Almighty', in place of: consubstantial with the Almighty, breathed out of his hypostasis; so that even one such naming alone shows him both consubstantial with God the Father and sanctifying and not contained even by reason. Accordingly, the one able both to speak and to set out patterns of faith, Paul [...]
pass_b_english: … you were sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11). Observe, then, observe: if the name of the Son is a divine name, as indeed it is, then beyond all doubt so is the name of the Holy Spirit; for he made plain one name belonging to both. Observe too that the Holy Spirit, as he ineffably shared in creating at the beginning, now also creates anew; for “to be washed” signified “to be created anew”. And to Titus he writes: “having begotten us again through the washing of rebirth and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5). The sacred psalmist, no less, would have us know that those who already exist by birth are now being created spiritually in the divine font. For he says: “A people that is being created will praise the Lord” (Psalm 102:18).

So, then, the hypostases that have the same honour and the same working have received the same nature as their portion. They differ from one another in nothing, in Godhead or in power, and they alone can be naturally joined with the One, ranked with him, and everywhere conceived together with him. He it is who has both from himself, without beginning, on equal and like terms, united with him and bound to him in a way past speaking, though he himself is not the hypostases of the two.

Further, besides what has been said: every plea of these heretics follows the same pattern, and uses the same words, as the stale sophistry of theirs that is now in motion; we shall learn this by experience before long from the chapters themselves. For if some word, say “eternal” or “good”, which carries a divine meaning about the Trinity in unity and belongs to it wholly and perfectly, happens to have been said somewhere of a creature, with the qualification proper to a creature, they say nothing about God the Father and his Son (what indeed could they say?); but at once, most senselessly, they bring the Holy Spirit down to the creation, instead of raising him, as is most fitting, to God and the Only-begotten, whom the theologians have most aptly praised in like and equal terms with the Holy Spirit.

Now the arguments we have put forward in the chapter we are pursuing cannot, even on their own, be got past, and they suffice for the whole contest with the heretics. So either let them show (a thing very grievous even to say) that a beginning or an end of the Holy Spirit has been declared anywhere in the oracles; or that he had any road at all toward corruption, as angelic and human choice has; or else, as the saying goes, let “an ox stand on their tongue”. So much for them. I shall now pass on to the subject I set out from.
That, being unchangeable, he admits neither virtue nor vice.

The rational creation admits both virtue and vice. Among the bodiless, as we said before, we find the approved angels within virtue and those cast out within vice; and so too among beings in bodies, such as we ourselves are. But the divine Spirit is above virtue and glory, or rather is himself the spring from which the highest virtue flows, and he admits none of these, as neither does the Father nor the Son. If he does not admit them, neither is his will other than theirs; and if that is so (for he does all that the Father wills), neither is his substance other. From this, then, two things are gathered: that he is not a creature, but stands toward God the Father and his Son without any difference; and that through him we know that God, from whom he proceeded by nature, is in us too, as it is written (1 John 3:24).
That he is holy by nature, and sanctifies and justifies.

Creation is sanctified and justified by God, who is holy by nature; for it is able to receive sanctification and justification, not to bestow them. But the Holy Spirit stands apart from creation and is joined by nature to him from whom he has proceeded, the one about whom we were taught in the mysteries that “every good giving and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning” (James 1:17). He cares and provides for all, even for the guilty. So he sanctifies, justifies and makes wise, and furnishes every form of heavenly virtue; but he himself is in no way found to have any capacity to be sanctified, justified or made wise by another, just as neither has the self-existent Father nor his Son, who shares his nature. For this reason too he is rightly praised as holy in himself and as “Spirit of holiness” (Romans 1:4), that is, holy by nature and of himself; as “divine Spirit”, that is, God by nature; and as “breath of the Almighty” (Job 33:4), that is, consubstantial with the Almighty, breathed forth from his hypostasis. Even one such name, then, taken alone, shows him to be consubstantial with God the Father, and sanctifying, and beyond the reach even of reason. Accordingly Paul, mighty both to speak and to set out the patterns of the faith, …

choices.issue: Old draft garbled, wrong references, chapter title run in
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English rendered ἡγιάσθητε 'you were baptized', συγκτίσαν ('having co-created') 'having gathered them', κολυμβήθρα 'swimming pool', ὑπὲρ ἀρετήν ('above virtue') 'participating in virtue', ἑτερόβουλον ('of another will') 'of a different substance', οὐ παρεκτική ('not able to bestow') 'not incapable', ὑπαιτίων ('the guilty') 'the lowly', μηδὲ λόγῳ χωρεῖσθαι 'not contained by the Word', δικαιολογηθέντων 'having been justified'; it ran the 6.5ν chapter title into a sentence ('the initial hypothesis: that as it is unchangeable'), split 'an ox on the tongue' from its clause, and dropped the conclusion that we know God is in us. References fixed: 'Psalm 50:2' for Greek Psalm 101:19 (now Psalm 102:18); '1 Cor 6:19' for 'as it is written' (now 1 John 3:24). Added 1 Corinthians 6:11, Romans 1:4, Job 33:4. Bracket fillers [the old], [praises], [nature] removed. Chapter titles 6.5ν and 6.6ν stand as their own paragraphs. Ends mid-sentence as the Greek does.

choices.english: … you were sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ
choices.why: The quotation of 1 Corinthians 6:11 began in the previous section; only this section's words are translated, and the reference is given where the quotation ends.

choices.term: ἓν γὰρ ἀμφοῖν αὐτῶν ἐδήλωσεν ὄνομα
choices.english: for he made plain one name belonging to both
choices.why: The subject is Paul, whose verse joins 'the name of the Lord Jesus Christ' and 'the Spirit of our God' under one 'in'.

choices.english: And to Titus he writes
choices.why: Answers Κορινθίοις μέν in the previous section ('to the Corinthians … and to Titus'); 'he writes' carried over from that verb.

choices.english: The sacred psalmist, no less, would have us know
choices.why: ἀξιοῖ εἰδέναι: he deems it right that we know; 'would have us know'.

choices.english: So, then
choices.why: Read as the inferential οὐκοῦν; the copy-text accent would make it a rhetorical question ('Do not then …?'), which comes to the same affirmation.

choices.term: ὃς ἄμφω αὐτός, οὐχ ὧν αἱ ὑποστάσεις ἀμφοῖν, ἔχει ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ …
choices.english: He it is who has both from himself … though he himself is not the hypostases of the two
choices.why: The copy-text ὧν gives no sense; read as ὤν ('not being'): the One (the Father) has the Son and the Spirit from himself without being identical with them. See problems.

choices.english: follows the same pattern, and uses the same words
choices.why: Two coined parallels (same manner, same wording); kept as a pair.

choices.english: with the qualification proper to a creature
choices.why: μνήμη here is the mention or framing that a word receives when applied to a creature.

choices.english: whom the theologians have most aptly praised in like and equal terms with the Holy Spirit
choices.why: The masculine plural refers to God and the Only-begotten; the object of ἀνάγουσι is the Spirit, carried over from κατάγουσι. 'The theologians' are the inspired writers.

choices.english: let “an ox stand on their tongue”
choices.why: A Greek proverb for enforced silence (a heavy weight on the tongue); kept as a saying, the meaning clear from 'or else'.

choices.english: the subject I set out from
choices.why: ὑπόθεσις here is the subject of the treatise, not a 'hypothesis'.

choices.term: ἐν δὲ σώμασιν, ὡς ἐσμὲν ἡμεῖς αὐτοί
choices.english: and so too among beings in bodies, such as we ourselves are
choices.why: The μέν/δέ contrast is bodiless and embodied rational beings.

choices.term: μᾶλλον δ' αὐτὸ πηγάζον τὴν ἀκροτάτην ἀρετήν
choices.english: or rather is himself the spring from which the highest virtue flows
choices.why: πηγάζω: to pour forth as a spring.

choices.term: τὸ ἡμᾶς ἐξ αὐτοῦ τὸν θεόν … γινώσκειν, ὅτι καὶ ἐν ἡμῖν ἐστιν ὡς γέγραπται
choices.english: that through him we know that God, from whom he proceeded by nature, is in us too, as it is written (1 John 3:24)
choices.why: 'God' is drawn forward as object of 'know' ahead of the 'that' clause; the verse is 1 John 3:24 (we know that he abides in us by the Spirit he has given us).

choices.english: not to bestow them
choices.why: παρεκτικός: able to furnish or bestow; set against δεκτική ('receptive').

choices.english: we were taught in the mysteries
choices.why: Initiation teaching (baptismal catechesis).

choices.english: justified
choices.why: 59 is a printed page number in the copy-text; page debris, omitted.

choices.term: ὁ αὐτοφυὴς πατὴρ … ὁ ὁμοφυὴς αὐτοῦ υἱός
choices.english: the self-existent Father … his Son, who shares his nature
choices.why: ὁμοφυής is 'of the same nature', distinct from ὁμοούσιος ('consubstantial') used a few lines later.

choices.english: holy in himself
choices.why: Compound 'self-holy': holy not by participation.

choices.english: beyond the reach even of reason
choices.why: λόγος here is human reason or speech, not the divine Word; 'not contained even by reason'.

choices.english: Accordingly Paul, mighty both to speak and to set out the patterns of the faith, …
choices.why: The sentence runs on into the next section; only this section's words are translated, with a closing ellipsis.
